title: だ / です — “A is B”
summary: だ and です both mean “to be” and close a sentence of the type “A is B.” です is the polite form, だ is the plain (casual) form. They attach to a noun (and to a na-adjective stem).

patterns.gloss: Polite: Noun + です (e.g. 学生です)
Plain: Noun + だ (e.g. 日曜日だ)

body.p: Japanese does not use a verb like “be” in the same way as English. Instead, you put です (polite) or だ (plain) after a noun to say what something is: これは本です, 今日は日曜日だ. It is often paired with は, which marks the topic.

Use です with teachers, strangers, customers and in most everyday polite speech. Use だ with close friends and family, in diaries, and inside longer sentences written in plain style. The meaning is the same; only the level of politeness changes.

The negative is ではありません／じゃありません (polite) and ではない／じゃない (plain); the past is でした (polite) and だった (plain). In plain speech, the final だ is often dropped or replaced by particles such as ね and よ, and men tend to use だ more directly than women do.

examples.note: Noun + です is the basic polite “A is B” sentence.

examples.ja: 私（わたし）は学生（がくせい）です。
examples.note: は marks the topic “I”; です says what I am.

examples.ja: 今日（きょう）は日曜日（にちようび）だ。
examples.note: だ is the plain form; the meaning is the same as 日曜日です.

pitfalls: です and だ attach to nouns and na-adjective stems, not directly to verbs. Do not say 食べるです; say 食べます or 食べる. (For i-adjectives, 高いです is fine, but 高いだ is not.)
Do not use だ when speaking politely to a teacher or a stranger; choose です.
